name: Tip of the tongue
statement: A person who cannot retrieve a word can often report parts of it, its first letter above all, at rates above the words that come to mind in its place.
meaning: The tip of the tongue state is a retrieval failure with a peculiar shape. The word will not come, the speaker is sure it is known, and recall feels about to happen. Brown and McNeill called what the speaker can produce meanwhile generic recall: a letter or two, a syllable count, a stress pattern, sometimes a suffix. This is a memory phenomenon and not a bias. Nothing about it makes judgement systematically wrong, and it earns a place here because of what it has been taken to prove about the mental lexicon. If meaning can be retrieved while sound cannot, then meaning and sound are stored separately and reached in that order. Two rival readings of the failure have driven the field. On the blocking account a wrong word arrives first and jams the search. On the transmission deficit account nothing jams anything, and the sound of the word is simply activated too weakly to be selected. The evidence has moved a long way towards the second.

origin.where: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior
origin.note: Brown and McNeill did not discover the state, they made it happen on demand. Their paper opens with a passage they date to 1893 in which William James describes 'a gap that is intensely active'. They credit earlier naturalistic records to Woodworth in 1934 and to Wenzl in 1932 and 1936, and dismiss them as unsystematic: several months of watching themselves and asking their friends yielded fewer than a dozen good cases. Reading out definitions of rare words was the method that changed that.

evidence: Brown and McNeill ran a pretest on nine people interviewed for two hours each, which produced 57 tip of the tongue states. Guesses at the number of syllables were right 47% of the time and guesses at the first letter 51%. The main experiment used 56 Harvard and Radcliffe undergraduates in three two-hour evening sessions and a list of 49 words drawn from a Thorndike-Lorge frequency band, among them apse, nepotism, cloaca, ambergris and sampan. It produced 360 signalled states, of which 233 were positive, meaning the target was known and the guesses could be scored. Participants also listed the words that came to mind, 224 judged similar in sound and 95 judged similar in meaning, and the similar-meaning words serve as the baseline. Explicit guesses at the number of syllables were correct 57% of the time, and the modes of the guesses matched the true count exactly for one, two and three syllables. The similar-sounding words matched the target's syllable count in 48% of cases against 20% for the similar-meaning words. The first letter was guessed correctly 57% of the time, or 62% counting each word once. Similar-sounding words matched the target's first letter in 49% of cases; similar-meaning words managed 8%. Accuracy tracked nearness to the target. Among states that ended when the experimenter read the word out, 58 of 138 first-letter guesses were right, 42%. Among states where the participant recalled the intended word unaided it was 20 of 36, 56%, and where the participant recalled a different target of their own, 39 of 59, 66%. Endings behaved like chunks: of 93 similar-sounding words produced for a target ending in a suffix, 30 matched its last three letters, against 5 of 130 for targets with no suffix. The states were not evenly distributed. Nine participants had none at all in two hours and the most anyone had was eight. Brown and McNeill call this the fragmentary data problem and report that no significance test is clearly appropriate to it. The blocking account was tested directly and did not survive. Jones read 40 definitions to 116 Bristol undergraduates, pairing each with a word related to the answer in sound, in meaning, in both or in neither. He recorded 457 states over 4,640 trials, 9.8%, and states ran higher when the paired word was related in sound, 62.1% against 37.9%, min F'(1,50) = 5.74. They also ran higher when the word followed the definition than when it preceded it, 59.1% against 40.9%. Perfect and Hanley reran the design with a no-interloper control. Their first experiment, on 58 staff and students at Liverpool, found that Jones's phonologically cued definitions produced more states with no interloper present at all, F(1,56) = 32.35. In two further experiments, with definitions matched for the states they produced unaided, the interlopers did nothing. Meyer and Bock reached the same place from another direction with 411, 348 and 261 participants across three experiments. Rotating every definition through every cue condition, sound cues helped: 1,013 correct targets after phonological cues, 951 after semantic and 917 after unrelated, with tip of the tongue states running the other way at 628, 682 and 658. Cueing only after a failed first attempt gave 108, 49 and 28 late retrievals for the three cue types. Their third experiment copied Jones's design, assigning each definition to one condition only, and reproduced his result, 375 correct targets after phonological cues against 577 after unrelated ones. The uncued data explain why. Jones's phonological items were retrieved from the definition alone 43.5% of the time, against 74.0% for his unrelated items, so the cue was carrying the blame for the words. Burke, MacKay, Worthley and Wade built the transmission deficit account on a diary study. Fifty young, 30 midage and 50 older adults kept structured diaries for 28 consecutive days and recorded 686 states, of which 653, or 95%, were resolved inside the four weeks. Mean counts were 3.92 for the young, 5.40 for the midage and 6.56 for the old, F(2,124) = 10.63. Older adults reported less partial information per state, 1.53 characteristics against 2.07 in the young, F(2,127) = 4.39, and fewer accompanying alternate words. States with a persistent alternate took longer to resolve in every age group, 13.3 minutes against 3.8 in the young, 12.5 against 4.9 in the midage and 51.1 against 15.8 in the old. Of the 33 states left unresolved, 18 had alternates and 15 did not. James and Burke tested the transmission deficit account by having 36 young adults and 36 adults with a mean age of 72 read aloud lists that shared phonemes with an answer they were about to be asked for. Prior production of those sounds cut tip of the tongue states, from a mean of 6.69 to 5.86 in the young and 7.86 to 6.44 in the older group, F1(1,70) = 6.34. In a second experiment the priming came only after retrieval had already failed, and it lifted resolution for states already in progress but not for questions answered 'don't know', F(1,31) = 7.19. Kornell and Metcalfe attacked the folklore about blockers from the resolution side. Sixty-four Columbia students sat their first experiment and 56 met its inclusion criterion. Delay helped tip of the tongue states resolve, and blocked states resolved less often than unblocked ones, but delay did not help blocked states more, F(1,55) = 1.23. In a second experiment on 60 students, reminding people of the word that had been blocking them changed resolution not at all, F(1,36) = 0.02.

examples.tag: The actor from the thing with the boat
examples.text: The name will not come, and what does come is that it starts with an M, has two syllables and ends in a vowel sound. A wrong name keeps arriving and will not clear. The wrong name is a symptom of the search failing, not the reason it failed.

examples.tag: The kitchen implement with no name
examples.text: Someone reaches for the word for the flat tool used to lift biscuits off a tray, produces the shape of the word, the number of beats in it and nothing else. The definition is intact and the sound is the part that will not activate.

A man recognises a classmate, knows where she sat, knows her surname was short and began with a hard sound, and cannot say it. Being sure it is known is a feeling about the search, and the feeling can appear for words that are not there at all.

replication.headline: Partial recall during the state reproduces across labs, languages and even a signed language; what has not reproduced is the explanation that a competing word causes it.
replication.detail: Koriat and Lieblich ran a modified version of the Brown and McNeill procedure on 56 Hebrew University students whose first language was English, using a 62-word list taken from Brown and McNeill. They signalled 772 states and report the findings generally replicated, with correct detection over positive states at 71% for first letters, 69% for last letters and 80% for syllable counts, against the 57% Brown and McNeill printed for first letters and for syllables. The same paper adds the qualification that has taken half a century to be absorbed: correct partial information also appeared when participants said they did not know the word at all, at 10% for first letters, 17% for last letters and 38% for syllable counts. Koriat and Lieblich separate detection based on the class a word belongs to from detection specific to that word, and find both in tip of the tongue states and in don't-know states. They also report that the high overall rates rest mostly on states where the participant's own target differed from the one the experimenter intended, which make up 72% of positive states. Brennen, Vikan and Dybdahl took the procedure to speakers of Q'eqchi', an unwritten Mayan language of Guatemala, testing illiterates, unschooled literates and schooled readers. Q'eqchi' has little sign of a dedicated expression for the state, yet most participants in all three groups recognised a description of it, states were induced in all three groups, and presenting the word's initials reliably resolved them. Only the university-level participants reported partial knowledge of words they had failed to recall. Thompson, Emmorey and Gollan elicited the same state in deaf signers of American Sign Language, where it is a tip of the fingers. Signers were likelier to retrieve a target sign's handshape, location and orientation than its movement, and often recalled the first letter of a fingerspelled word. Brown's 1991 review of the literature summarises the state as nearly universal, occurring about once a week, rising with age, often triggered by proper names, and resolved about half the time while it is happening.

study.cite: Koriat, A., & Lieblich, I. (1974). What does a person in a 'TOT' state know that a person in a 'don't know' state doesn't know. Memory & Cognition, 2(4), 647-655.

limits: The state is easy to elicit and hard to measure cleanly. Brown and McNeill's own design gives unequal numbers of observations per word and per person, and they say plainly that they know of no significance test they can be sure is appropriate. Their 57% for first letters is scored over positive states only, those where the target turned out to be known. It carries no stated chance baseline. The 8% for similar-meaning words is the comparison they offer, and they say the true chance level is unknown. Later figures are not comparable to it. Meyer and Bock subtracted an estimate of guessing from the cue word itself. In their first experiment that left accurate first letters at 18%, 21% and 20% of states and accurate syllable counts at 18%, 27% and 26%, for phonological, semantic and unrelated cues, computed over the states reported in each condition rather than over scorable ones. Ageing is where the measurement problem bites hardest. Burke and colleagues' diary counts rose with age, and a hierarchical regression left age the only predictor of them once vocabulary, education and digit span had been entered. Dahlgren put three cohorts, aged 17 to 29, 30 to 49 and 50 to 82, through 57 general knowledge questions, found the same raw age effect, and lost it to an analysis of covariance on level of knowledge. His argument is that older participants know more of the words that can go missing. James and Burke's own first experiment found no significant age effect on the number of states, F1(1,70) = 1.04, and they say they had picked questions that minimise it. The age gap they do report, 12.4% against 19.1% in their second experiment, F1(1,34) = 4.59, p < .05, is states as a proportion of unsuccessful retrievals rather than a raw count. Schwartz's language survey is a survey of informants, not of a sampled set of languages, and the paper does not say how many speakers were consulted for each. Its text names five languages that do not use the tongue metaphor while its Appendix A lists six, adding Amharic. The Huebert, McNeely-White and Cleary paper was read as an abstract only, as were Brennen and colleagues, Thompson and colleagues, Dahlgren, Schwartz's illusory-states paper and Brown's review. The published text of James and Burke was not obtained, and every figure attributed to them here is read off the authors' own posted manuscript. No meta-analysis of tip of the tongue states was found. The search ran on 21 September 2026 over Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed, OpenAlex and the open web, and turned up narrative reviews, an edited volume and a 2025 book but no quantitative synthesis, so no pooled effect size is given anywhere on this page.
misreadings: The finding is routinely inflated into proof that the missing word is sitting in storage, fully formed, with a lock on the door. It shows something narrower. Schwartz induced states for questions that had no answer, and every one of his 31 participants in that experiment reported at least one such illusory state. A feeling that a word is about to arrive is evidence about the feeling. Partial information is also read as something the state confers. Koriat and Lieblich found correct partial detection in people who said they did not know the word. Huebert, McNeely-White and Cleary report that under free report, people give more partial-recall responses during these states without being more accurate in them. Forced to guess a first letter, their participants claimed to know it while getting it wrong. Brennen and colleagues found partial knowledge reported only by their university-educated Q'eqchi' speakers, though the state itself and its resolution by initials appeared in every group. A third error takes Brown and McNeill's headline figure at face value. Jones reads the proximity data on their page 332 as giving 50.2% correct first-letter guesses, against the 57% printed on page 329, and suggests the larger figure was confused with the one for syllables. The blocker story is the most durable error. Jones found that sound-alike words presented with a definition increase the rate of these states. Perfect and Hanley found the higher rate again in the same definitions with no interloper attached, and Meyer and Bock found that Jones's phonological definitions were the hardest to answer before any cue arrived. James and Burke wrote in 2000 that the blocking explanation has a tenacious hold and is widely cited despite the absence of supporting evidence. Kornell and Metcalfe later showed that pushing a person's own blocker back in front of them does nothing to their chance of resolving the state. Blockers arrive because retrieval is failing; they are a symptom. The claim that almost every language calls this the tip of the tongue is repeated without its source and is close to true. Schwartz's informants covered 51 languages, and 45 of them use a tongue metaphor. American Sign Language, Icelandic, Kiswahili, Kalenjin and Indonesian do not, five languages including Cantonese, Mandarin, Hindi, Hausa and Ibo say the word is in the mouth, and Japanese puts it out of the throat. Korean, which supplied Schwartz's title, has it sparkling at the end of the tongue.

sources.text: Brown, R., & McNeill, D. (1966). The 'tip of the tongue' phenomenon. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 5(4), 325-337. Read in full from a scanned copy; the source for every figure in the first half of the evidence section.

Koriat, A., & Lieblich, I. (1974). What does a person in a 'TOT' state know that a person in a 'don't know' state doesn't know. Memory & Cognition, 2(4), 647-655. Read in full from the publisher's open PDF; the source for the 772 states and for the don't-know detection rates.

Jones, G. V. (1989). Back to Woodworth: Role of interlopers in the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon. Memory & Cognition, 17(1), 69-76. Read in full from the publisher's open PDF; the source for the 457 states, the interloper effects and the 50.2% recount of Brown and McNeill.

Perfect, T. J., & Hanley, J. R. (1992). The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon: Do experimenter-presented interlopers have any effect? Cognition, 45(1), 55-75. Abstract read at PubMed and the text read from a reposted scan; the publisher's copy is closed.

Meyer, A. S., & Bock, K. (1992). The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon: Blocking or partial activation? Memory & Cognition, 20(6), 715-726. Read in full from the authors' posted copy; the source for all three experiments' counts.

Burke, D. M., MacKay, D. G., Worthley, J. S., & Wade, E. (1991). On the tip of the tongue: What causes word finding failures in young and older adults? Journal of Memory and Language, 30(5), 542-579. The origin of the transmission deficit account. Closed at the publisher and obtained instead as a scan of the first author's departmental copy, archived at the Internet Archive, and read from the page images.

James, L. E., & Burke, D. M. (2000). Phonological priming effects on word retrieval and tip-of-the-tongue experiences in young and older adults. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 26(6), 1378-1391. Read in full from the authors' own posted manuscript, which carries this citation. The publisher's PDF is blocked by a bot challenge rather than a paywall, so the published text was not compared against the manuscript.

Kornell, N., & Metcalfe, J. (2006). 'Blockers' do not block recall during tip-of-the-tongue states. Metacognition and Learning, 1(3), 248-261. Received June 2006, accepted and published online 24 February 2007. Read in full from an archived copy of the first author's posted PDF; the live copy now returns a bot challenge.

Schwartz, B. L. (1999). Sparkling at the end of the tongue: The etiology of tip-of-the-tongue phenomenology. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 6(3), 379-393. Read in full; the source for the 51-language survey and its exceptions.

Brennen, T., Vikan, R., & Dybdahl, R. (2007). Are tip-of-the-tongue states universal? Evidence from the speakers of an unwritten language. Memory, 15(2), 167-176. Abstract read.

On the relationship between tip-of-the-tongue states and partial recollective experience: Illusory partial recollective access during tip-of-the-tongue states. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 152(2), 542-570. Abstract read; the full text is behind a paywall.
Brown, A. S. (1991). A review of the tip-of-the-tongue experience. Psychological Bulletin, 109(2), 204-223. Abstract read.
